claims.proposition_evaluated: Edmonton's automated counters recorded nearly 1.3 million cycling trips in the first seven months of 2026 — operationalized per the brief as the sum of bicycle counts recorded by the City of Edmonton's automated bicycle counters between 2026-01-01 and 2026-07-31 inclusive, across every counter the City publishes in that window, in dataset tq23-qn4m.
claims.interpretation_notes: I queried the base dataset directly through the City's Socrata API rather than relying on any published summary. Sum of total_cyclist_count for log_timestamp from 2026-01-01T00:00:00 to 2026-07-31T23:45:00 inclusive = 1,291,714, over 933,576 fifteen-minute records at 48 counter locations. That is 0.6 percent below the stated 1.3 million. It falls inside the primary Supported band (at least 1.10 million, below 1.50 million) and also inside the tighter alternative Supported band (at least 1.17 million, below 1.43 million), so the verdict is not definition-sensitive across the two cutoff sets the brief fixes. The short-window rule does not trigger: the published record covers the full window, with records on all 212 calendar days and a last record at 2026-07-31T23:45. Two independently published City views agree exactly — the 15-minute dataset tq23-qn4m and the derived daily dataset sw7k-ptx8 both return 1,291,714 for the window. On the brief's instruction to use the City's own word: the City calls these counts, not trips. The dataset is titled 'Bike and Pedestrian Counts (Eco Counter)' and the field is 'Total Cyclist Count'; the word 'trips' comes from CBC News, whose sentence of 2026-08-07 the commenter reposted verbatim, and CBC itself writes that the counters 'measure the number of bikes that cross them, so the data is a better indicator of traffic volume than individual cyclists'. Under the brief's ladder that wording is a reporting requirement and a limitation, not a component of the verdict, which is set on the figure alone. Robustness check the brief does not require: excluding every record the City flags in out_of_service ('Outage 1', 44,973 records carrying 25,341 counts; 'Out of Service', 2,400 records carrying 1,349 counts) lowers the total to 1,265,024, still Supported under both cutoff sets.

supporting_evidence.finding: Sum of total_cyclist_count in the City's Eco-Counter dataset for 2026-01-01T00:00:00 through 2026-07-31T23:45:00 is 1,291,714, from 933,576 fifteen-minute records; the earliest record in the window is 2026-01-01T00:00:00 and the latest is 2026-07-31T23:45:00.

supporting_evidence.finding: The window is fully published, not a subtotal of a short window. Records exist on all 212 days from 2026-01-01 to 2026-07-31, no day has a zero network count, and the dataset as a whole runs to 2026-09-02T23:45. Monthly network totals: January 45,386; February 47,289; March 77,585; April 115,435; May 340,064; June 282,395; July 383,560.

supporting_evidence.quote: The dataset contains bicycle-only or combined bicycle and pedestrian counts monitored at multiple locations along Edmonton bike lanes and key traffic areas. Raw data from monitoring equipment has not undergone quality control processes.

supporting_evidence.finding: The exact sentence the commenter posted five times originates with CBC News, published 2026-08-07 and last modified 2026-08-31: 'CBC News analyzed the daily counts from Jan. 1, 2019, to July 31, 2026. Data suggests total cycling traffic has increased each of the past four years — and nearly 1.3 million trips have happened through the first seven months of 2026.'
supporting_evidence.source_title: Are people actually using Edmonton's bike lanes? Here's a look at the numbers
supporting_evidence.establishes: Where the circulating figure came from and that it is an analysis of the City's open dataset, not a City publication. It is a lead to the dataset, not the verdict source; the verdict figure is computed from tq23-qn4m directly.

challenging_evidence.finding: The City labels the data raw and unassured: 'Raw data from monitoring equipment has not undergone quality control processes,' and notes a full day's data may be incomplete due to technical, environmental or equipment failure. The City also told CBC after publication that pedestrian and cyclist counts had been unintentionally switched at three collection sites, most notably Queen Elizabeth Park, though it said the error affected only data prior to 2023.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Bike and Pedestrian Counts (Eco Counter), dataset tq23-qn4m — dataset description; and CBC editor's note
challenging_evidence.source_publisher: City of Edmonton Open Data Portal; CBC News
challenging_evidence.source_date: Dataset description retrieved 2026-09-03; CBC editor's note as of 2026-08-31
challenging_evidence.establishes: That the total is a raw, unaudited instrument reading. It lowers confidence in the exact digits, not in the order of magnitude or the band the total sits in. The disclosed error is stated to be confined to pre-2023 data and so does not touch the 2026 window.
challenging_evidence.quote: After publication, the City of Edmonton discovered issues with data prior to 2023 at three locations.

challenging_evidence.finding: The instrument counts passages, not trips or people. 383 of 10,176 possible counter-days in the window are missing (3.8 percent), spread over 7 of 48 counters, and 47,373 records carrying 26,690 cyclist counts are flagged by the City as 'Outage 1' or 'Out of Service'. One counter, 103 Street N of 102 Avenue, first appears on 2026-05-07, part-way through the window; one counter present in the same window of 2025, 106 Street N of Jasper Avenue, does not appear in 2026 at all.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Bike and Pedestrian Counts (Eco Counter), dataset tq23-qn4m — per-counter and per-day coverage queries
challenging_evidence.source_publisher: City of Edmonton Open Data Portal
challenging_evidence.establishes: That the published total is an incomplete and unstable census of passages past a changing set of fixed points. Missing days can only add to the total, so the direction of this uncertainty is upward, away from the lower cutoff and toward but far from the upper one.

challenging_evidence.finding: The same window in the two preceding years produced higher totals: 2025-01-01 to 2025-07-31, 1,611,749 counts from 936,958 records; 2024-01-01 to 2024-07-31, 1,547,532 counts from 964,411 records. The 2026 figure is 19.9 percent below 2025 and 16.5 percent below 2024 (reviewer's calculation). Full calendar years: 2022, 2,193,450; 2023, 2,468,946; 2024, 2,772,283; 2025, 2,856,631.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Bike and Pedestrian Counts (Eco Counter), dataset tq23-qn4m — prior-year window and annual queries
challenging_evidence.source_publisher: City of Edmonton Open Data Portal
challenging_evidence.establishes: Scale for the 2026 figure. This does not challenge the proposition, which is about the 2026 figure alone, but it does challenge the growth gloss that travelled with it: CBC's 'increased each of the past four years' holds on calendar-year totals through 2025 and does not hold for the 2026 seven-month window against the same window in either of the two prior years.

limitations: The City's word for what these records are is 'count', not 'trip'. The dataset is 'Bike and Pedestrian Counts (Eco Counter)' and the field is 'Total Cyclist Count'. 'Trips' is CBC's word and the commenter's. A passage past a fixed point is not a person and not a journey: a rider passing the same counter to work and home is two counts, one journey past two counters is two counts, and a ride where there is no counter is none. The verdict is on the figure, and the figure is 1,291,714 published bicycle counts.

The dataset is tq23-qn4m, rows last updated 2026-09-03T22:53:20Z, created 2023-06-21, and it was the newest release of this data on the as-of date. The counter-locations dataset py7x-4d39 (59 rows, last updated 2026-09-03T22:53:24Z) was consulted only to confirm it carries no facility-type field; the counts dataset publishes its own latitude and longitude and I used those. The derived daily view sw7k-ptx8 was used only as a cross-check and returns the same total.

Counter coverage in the window: 48 distinct counter locations reported, of which 41 have a cyclist-capable counter_configuration ('Cyclist Only', 'Cyclist and Pedestrian', 'Cyclist and e-Scooter') and 7 are configured 'Pedestrian' and contribute zero to the total. 41 of the 48 published all 212 days.

Qualification 3, bounded absence: I found no City of Edmonton publication of this seven-month 2026 network total. I searched data.edmonton.ca (dataset pages and derived views including 'Monthly Pedestrian and Bicycle Counts Chart' 4r9q-db3a and 'Monthly Bike Counts by Location' gm5u-psbx, and the portal story 'Cycling in Edmonton' ktwr-rn4x, which loaded without content) and searched the web for an edmonton.ca figure, on 2026-09-03. The City publishes the data; the seven-month total appears to have been computed by CBC. I did not find it stated by the City, which is not the same as its not existing.

Qualification 4, the on-street versus off-street split: the counter-locations dataset py7x-4d39 has no facility-type field, so the City's locations data does not allow the split on its own. I computed it myself by joining each cyclist-capable counter's published latitude and longitude to the nearest Bike Routes segment (vd4b-a4iv) with route_coming_soon false, using the segment 'type' field. Reviewer's calculation: 20 on-road counters carry 646,365 counts (50.0 percent of the window total) and 21 off-road counters carry 645,349 (50.0 percent). The busiest single counter, High Level Bridge West, is off-road (Shared Pathway) and carries 127,740, or 9.9 percent of the total (reviewer's calculation, 127,740 / 1,291,714). My join used a 300-metre pre-filter on segment endpoints and a flat local projection at latitude 53.54; every matched distance was under 25 metres, so the approximation does not affect the classification. This split is context and carries no part of the verdict.

This claim and claim 2 (bike-lanes-look-empty) both rest on dataset tq23-qn4m. This claim takes a network total over seven months of 2026; claim 2 takes daily rates at named corridors in 2025. Neither finding evidences the other, and my facility-type join here is not a substitute for claim 2's five membership tests, which I did not run.
unknowns: How many distinct people the 1,291,714 counts represent. No counter can establish this and nothing published measures it.
How many of the counts are the same rider passing more than one counter on one journey, or the same rider passing one counter twice in a day. The dataset has no way to tell.

Whether the counters are accurately sited or calibrated, and whether a device fault explains any part of the year-over-year decline. Several counters with apparently full record coverage recorded far less in 2026 than in 2025 at the same site (102 Avenue E of 105 Street fell from 83,723 to 20,609; 102 Avenue SUP W of Groat Road Bridge from 61,210 to 19,315; Capilano SUP from 26,011 to 6,815), which is consistent with either a real drop or a partly failed sensor. The published record does not settle which, and this claim does not test it.
Whether the City's post-publication correction to pre-2023 data at three sites has been fully applied to the portal, and whether any further correction is pending for 2023 onward.
Whether the 26,690 counts sitting on records the City flags 'Outage 1' or 'Out of Service' should be counted. The City publishes them with values; I report the total both ways.

calculations_needed: Network total, 2026-01-01 to 2026-07-31: numerator 1,291,714 bicycle counts; no denominator, it is a raw count; geography City of Edmonton; instrument the City's automated Eco-Counter bicycle counters as published in tq23-qn4m; dataset last updated 2026-09-03.
Distance from the stated figure: 1,291,714 against 1,300,000 is 0.6 percent low (reviewer's calculation).
Same window, two preceding years: 2025, 1,611,749; 2024, 1,547,532. 2026 is 19.9 percent below 2025 and 16.5 percent below 2024 (reviewer's calculation).

Counters and gaps: 48 counter locations reported, 41 of them cyclist-capable; all 212 days present network-wide; 383 of 10,176 counter-days missing, 3.8 percent (reviewer's calculation); one counter added on 2026-05-07; one counter present in the 2025 window absent from the 2026 window.
Total excluding City-flagged outage records: 1,291,714 minus 26,690 equals 1,265,024 (reviewer's calculation).

Busiest counter share: 127,740 / 1,291,714 = 9.9 percent (reviewer's calculation). On-road counters 646,365 / 1,291,714 = 50.0 percent; off-road 645,349 / 1,291,714 = 50.0 percent (reviewer's calculation, method stated in limitations).
what_would_change_my_verdict: A City republication of tq23-qn4m that materially restates 2026 values, for example a further correction of the kind applied to the pre-2023 records at three sites, moving the window total outside 1.10 to 1.50 million.

Evidence that a substantial share of the 2026 counts are double counts introduced by an equipment or ingestion fault rather than by passages. A fault large enough to push the corrected total below 1.10 million would move the verdict to Partially supported.

A demonstration that my window boundary is wrong, for instance that log_timestamp is stored in a timezone that shifts records across the 2026-07-31 or 2026-01-01 boundary in a way that changes the total by more than a few thousand. Given the total sits 0.6 percent from the stated figure and roughly 16 percent from the nearest cutoff, only a large error would matter.

A finding that the correct reading of the proposition is the word 'trips' rather than the figure. Under that reading the counters would not establish trips at all, but the brief fixes the verdict on the figure and I have followed it.
claims.suggested_one_line: Edmonton's automated counters recorded 1,291,714 bicycle counts between January 1 and July 31, 2026, which is what 'nearly 1.3 million' describes — though the City's word is counts, not trips, and a count is a passage past a fixed point, not a person.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Yes, the figure checks out. Summing the City's own Eco-Counter dataset (tq23-qn4m) over 2026-01-01 to 2026-07-31 gives 1,291,714 bicycle counts, 0.6 percent below the stated 1.3 million, and the City's separate daily dataset returns exactly the same number. The window is fully published, with records on all 212 days. Three things belong beside it. The City calls these counts, not trips: a counter records a passage past a fixed point, so a rider passing one counter twice is two counts and a rider where there is no counter is none, and nobody can say how many distinct people the number represents. The City labels the data raw and unassured, and 3.8 percent of counter-days in the window are missing, which can only push the true total up. And the same seven months in 2025 recorded 1,611,749 and in 2024 recorded 1,547,532, so 2026 is down about 20 percent on last year even though the figure itself is accurate as stated.
suggested_tldr: Sum of the City's published counter data for 2026-01-01 to 2026-07-31: 1,291,714 bicycle counts, from 48 counter locations, 41 of them cyclist-capable.
That is 0.6 percent below 'nearly 1.3 million', inside the Supported band under both the primary and the tighter alternative cutoffs.
The window is complete: records on all 212 days, last record 2026-07-31 at 23:45. Two separate City datasets return the same total.
The City's word is 'count', not 'trip'. The figure counts passages past fixed points, not people and not journeys, and no counter can say how many riders it represents.
The data is raw and unassured; 383 of 10,176 counter-days are missing (3.8 percent), which can only add to the total.
For scale: the same seven months recorded 1,611,749 in 2025 and 1,547,532 in 2024. The 2026 figure is accurate and it is also about 20 percent below last year's.

Half the counted volume comes from on-street counters and half from off-street paths and bridges; the single busiest counter, High Level Bridge West, is a shared pathway and carries 9.9 percent of the total.
